title: Adapter
summary: Wrap a foreign interface so existing code can call it as if it were local.

parts.rule: An adapter translates an interface you do not want into the interface your code already uses. Keep it at the boundary around a vendor SDK, legacy service, or incompatible data format. The rest of the application should depend on your interface and should not know the foreign method names, units, or error codes.
parts.why: Without an adapter, vendor details spread through controllers and domain code. A later SDK change then becomes an application-wide edit. A small translation layer gives that change one home and gives tests a stable interface to fake. The tradeoff is another type and another mapping to maintain, so the boundary must be real.
parts.example: The application owns an EnergySensor interface with readCelsius(deviceId). A vendor SDK instead exposes fetchTemperature(id) and returns {value: 98.6, unit: "F", status: "ok"}. VendorMeterAdapter implements EnergySensor. It calls fetchTemperature once, rejects a non-ok status, and converts the successful value with (98.6 - 32) × 5 / 9 = 37.0. Callers receive 37.0°C and never import the vendor package. The adapter also maps error E_CONN to the application's SensorUnavailable error, so retry policy stays outside the SDK. Unit tests pin the translations: 32°F becomes 0°C, 212°F becomes 100°C, and E_CONN becomes SensorUnavailable. Six months later a second vendor returns Celsius in a field named reading. Add SecondVendorAdapter; the alerting and reporting services still call readCelsius. Notice what does not belong here: deciding that 37°C is unsafe is a domain rule, so the application handles it after the adapter returns. The adapter changes vocabulary and representation, not business policy.
parts.use: Use an adapter when the caller-facing interface is worth protecting from a dependency you cannot control. It fits third-party SDKs, legacy protocols, file-format conversion, and ports around infrastructure. Define the internal interface from the application's needs, then make the adapter perform the smallest complete translation.
parts.refuse: Skip the pattern when you own both interfaces and a direct rename solves the mismatch. Avoid chains of adapters that make a request hard to trace. If a wrapper adds logging or caching without changing the interface, it is closer to a decorator or proxy. Keep pricing, validation, and other business decisions out of the mapping layer.

body:
Rule. An adapter translates an interface you do not want into the interface your code already uses. Keep it at the boundary around a vendor SDK, legacy service, or incompatible data format. The rest of the application should depend on your interface and should not know the foreign method names, units, or error codes.

Why it matters. Without an adapter, vendor details spread through controllers and domain code. A later SDK change then becomes an application-wide edit. A small translation layer gives that change one home and gives tests a stable interface to fake. The tradeoff is another type and another mapping to maintain, so the boundary must be real.

Worked example. The application owns an EnergySensor interface with readCelsius(deviceId). A vendor SDK instead exposes fetchTemperature(id) and returns {value: 98.6, unit: "F", status: "ok"}. VendorMeterAdapter implements EnergySensor. It calls fetchTemperature once, rejects a non-ok status, and converts the successful value with (98.6 - 32) × 5 / 9 = 37.0. Callers receive 37.0°C and never import the vendor package. The adapter also maps error E_CONN to the application's SensorUnavailable error, so retry policy stays outside the SDK. Unit tests pin the translations: 32°F becomes 0°C, 212°F becomes 100°C, and E_CONN becomes SensorUnavailable. Six months later a second vendor returns Celsius in a field named reading. Add SecondVendorAdapter; the alerting and reporting services still call readCelsius. Notice what does not belong here: deciding that 37°C is unsafe is a domain rule, so the application handles it after the adapter returns. The adapter changes vocabulary and representation, not business policy.

[[diagram:adapt]]

When to use. Use an adapter when the caller-facing interface is worth protecting from a dependency you cannot control. It fits third-party SDKs, legacy protocols, file-format conversion, and ports around infrastructure. Define the internal interface from the application's needs, then make the adapter perform the smallest complete translation.

When to refuse. Skip the pattern when you own both interfaces and a direct rename solves the mismatch. Avoid chains of adapters that make a request hard to trace. If a wrapper adds logging or caching without changing the interface, it is closer to a decorator or proxy. Keep pricing, validation, and other business decisions out of the mapping layer.
